newsitem.title: USA: Olympic bombing ex-suspect felt like hunted animal.
newsitem.headline: Olympic bombing ex-suspect felt like hunted animal.

text.p: One-time Olympic security guard Richard Jewell said on Monday he felt like a "hunted animal" as the FBI and news media watched his every move following the July bombing that claimed two lives and injured more than 100.

Jewell, 33, brushing tears from his eyes and with his voice breaking, said he planned to try to find work again as a law enforcement officer. "I felt like a hunted animal, followed constantly, waiting to be killed," he said in a 15-minute speech to journalists.

He went from being a hero to the case's only named suspect in three days after the July 27 blast at Centennial Olympic Park in downtown Atlanta. He was finally cleared of suspicion on Saturday when the Justice Department issued a letter saying he was no longer a target of the FBI bomb investigation.

Jewell, flanked by an American flag as he spoke to scores of journalists from a podium in a hotel ballroom, called his experience "88 days of hell." He criticised the FBI investigation of him and the U.S. news media coverage.

"In their mad rush to fulfil their own personal agendas, the FBI and the media almost destroyed me and my mother" he said. "Now that I have received the government's letter, I feel a sense of relief," he said.
"After 88 days of hell, it is hard to believe it is really over ... I hope and pray that no one else is ever subjected to the pain and ordeal I have gone through.

"The media said I fitted the profile of a lone bomber. That was a lie. The media said I was a frustrated police wannabe. That was lie ... It was all a lie," he said. "I thank God that it has ended and that you all know what I have known all along -- I am an innocent man."

In a scathing attack, Jewell said investigators jumped to conclusions about his character and behaviour. He said he considered himself a professional law enforcement officer and was dedicated to protecting the public and saving lives.

The high-profile Olympics incident made Jewell and his mother Barbara virtual prisoners in their home. Whenever he left for any reason, including going to a baseball game, FBI agents and news media trailed his every move.

Although Jewell did not say in his 15-minute speech whether he planned to sue the U.S. government or any news media, his attorneys have hinted for weeks that lawsuits might be forthcoming to help clear his name and reputation.

Early on July 27, Jewell was working as a private security guard near Centennial Olympic Park when he spotted a suspicious green knapsack at a crowded outdoor concert. He alerted police and helped clear revellers from the area before a pipe bomb in the pack detonated.
The blast claimed two lives, a suburban Atlanta mother and a Turkish cameraman who was rushing to the scene. More than 100 people at the park were injured.
Jewell initially was hailed as a hero for his actions. But on July 30 an article in the Journal-Constitution named him as a focus of the investigation.

Within hours, the apartment complex where he lived was besieged by hundreds of journalists who stayed on to witness a mammoth FBI search in which federal agents hauled his property away in boxes. A troop of reporters remained at the site for weeks thereafter.
Despite reports that the FBI has identified half a dozen potential suspects in its ongoing probe, the investigation to date has shown no sign of closing in on the real bomber.
Earlier on Monday, the U.S. attorney's office in Atlanta released a copy of the FBI affidavit that cited circumstantial evidence as pointing to Jewell as a suspect early in the investigation.
